purpose: Find where the system is INSECURE WHEN NOBODY CONFIGURES IT, and where a failing security check lets the request through anyway. These are the bugs that ship silently, because nothing is broken on the developer's machine.
reading_rule: READ THE DEFAULT VALUE, NOT THE FLAG NAME. `verify_ssl` is an intention; `verify_ssl=False` is the behaviour. A config option existing is never a finding - its value is.
verify_before_reporting: V1 Is this actually the default in a real deployment, or is it overridden on every shipped path? If a shipped config sets a safe value everywhere, this is DEFENCE-IN-DEPTH at most - and you must name where the override lives.
V2 Is this path reachable in production, or is it dev-only and excluded from the build? Name the build flag, environment check or bundler exclusion that proves it.
V3 What does an attacker get if it stays at this value? If you cannot write that sentence, you have a code smell, not a finding.
reject_these_excuses: 'It is only the default, real deployments override it.' - then prove it: name the file that overrides it on EVERY shipped path. Undocumented overrides are how staging config reaches production.
'That branch is only for local development.' - then name the build-time exclusion. An `if DEBUG` that reads an env var is not an exclusion; it is a switch an attacker may be able to flip.
'The framework would never run with that setting in production.' - name the version and the mechanism that prevents it, or treat it as reachable.
'It fails open on purpose, for availability.' - that is a deliberate decision that must be written down and bounded. Undocumented fail-open is Law 4 broken.
'MD5 here is not security-relevant.' - possibly true. Read what the digest is used for FIRST. A cache key is fine; a token, signature or password is not.

rules.title: Secret read from the environment with a hardcoded fallback
rules.note: The fallback IS the production secret the first time someone forgets to set the variable, and it is in your git history forever. This is the single highest-value pattern in this pack.
rules.fix: Remove the fallback. Fail to start: read the variable, and if it is missing raise at boot. A process that will not start is a visible outage; a process running on a known default is a silent breach.

rules.title: Framework secret key set to a placeholder or example value
rules.note: A placeholder signing key means every session cookie and JWT in the deployment is forgeable by anyone who has read the repo or guessed the framework's tutorial value.
rules.fix: Generate a high-entropy key per environment, load it from a secret manager, and assert its length and entropy at startup.

rules.title: Default or well-known credentials in configuration
rules.note: Default credential pairs are the first thing any scanner tries. Check whether this file ships, or is only used by the local compose stack.
rules.fix: Require credentials to be supplied per environment, and make first-boot force a change. Never ship a working default account.

rules.title: TLS certificate verification disabled
rules.note: Turns every TLS connection on this path into an unauthenticated one. The encryption still happens, which is what makes it feel safe - but any network position can now impersonate the peer.
rules.fix: Verify by default. If a private CA is the real problem, install the CA bundle and keep verification on. Never disable verification globally to fix one endpoint.

rules.title: Authentication or authorisation check fails open
rules.note: Law 4. This is the highest-value shape in the whole pack and no regex finds it reliably - use this hit as a prompt to read every security decision and ask: what happens if it THROWS, TIMES OUT, or returns NULL?
rules.fix: Deny on every abnormal path. The catch block returns false, the timeout denies, and the null result denies. If availability genuinely requires fail-open, document it, bound it, and alarm on it.

rules.title: Debug or development mode enabled by default
rules.note: Debug mode typically means stack traces with source, an interactive console, verbose errors and disabled caching. In some frameworks the debugger is remote code execution by design.
rules.fix: Default to off. Read the flag from the environment with a SAFE default, and assert at startup that it is off when the deployment is not local.

rules.title: CORS configured to allow any origin
rules.note: Severity depends entirely on what else is true. A wildcard origin WITH credentials allowed is the serious case; browsers refuse that combination, so check whether the code reflects the Origin header back instead - that is the same bug wearing a disguise.
rules.fix: Allowlist the exact origins. If you must be dynamic, match against a fixed list; never echo the request's Origin header.

rules.title: Cookie missing Secure, HttpOnly or SameSite
rules.note: Read which cookie this is. A session or auth cookie without HttpOnly is stealable by any XSS; without Secure it leaks over plain HTTP; SameSite=None without Secure is rejected by modern browsers, so this may already be dead code.
rules.fix: For session and auth cookies: Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Lax or Strict. Use None only for a genuine cross-site flow, and then Secure is mandatory.

rules.title: Service bound to all interfaces or an admin port left open
rules.note: Inside a container this is usually correct and expected. On a host, or with host networking, it exposes the service to every reachable network. Check the deployment shape before you judge it.
rules.fix: Bind to localhost unless the service is meant to be reachable, and put the network boundary in the platform rather than in the application.

rules.title: Overly permissive file, bucket or object permissions
rules.note: World-writable is worse than world-readable: it means an attacker can replace content that something else trusts. Check who else reads the path or the bucket.
rules.fix: Least privilege (Law 8). 0600 for secrets, 0644 for read-only data, and a named principal instead of a wildcard.

rules.title: Weak or default cryptographic parameters
rules.note: Classify the purpose before judging: a low iteration count for password storage is serious; MD5 for a cache key is not a finding at all. Read what the value protects.
rules.fix: Use the current recommended parameters and put them in one place, so raising them later is a single change: Argon2id or bcrypt with a modern cost for passwords, RSA 3072+ or an elliptic curve for keys, and TLS 1.2 as the floor.

rules.title: No limit on request size, page size, upload or iteration
rules.note: Law 9. On its own this is availability and cost; combined with an expensive operation per item, or an agent loop, it becomes the actual bill. Note that a zero timeout usually means 'wait forever', not 'do not wait'.
rules.fix: Set an explicit bound on every list, body, upload, retry, loop and spend, and return a clear error when it is exceeded.

rules.title: Signature, token or integrity verification disabled by default
rules.note: If the verifier accepts the algorithm from the token, or accepts `none`, the signature is decoration. Check whether an attacker chooses the algorithm.
rules.fix: Pin the expected algorithm in the verifier, verify exp/aud/iss, and never accept `none`. Package integrity checks stay on.

rules.title: Security middleware, header or protection disabled
rules.note: Autoescape disabled is the highest-impact member of this group: it silently turns every template variable into an XSS sink (Law 6).
rules.fix: Keep the framework's protections on globally and make exemptions per-route, narrow, and commented with the reason.

rules.title: Insecure transport used by default
rules.note: A schema or namespace URL over http is not a transport finding. What matters is a real endpoint that carries credentials or data.
rules.fix: Use TLS for every non-loopback destination, and require it rather than negotiating down.

rules.title: Development or test bypass reachable in a shipped path
rules.note: The classic breach shape: a bypass added for local testing, guarded by a flag or header that turns out to be attacker-reachable. Answer V2 in writing - name the build-time exclusion, or treat it as production code.
rules.fix: Remove it, or exclude it at BUILD time rather than at runtime, so the code physically is not in the shipped artifact. A runtime flag is a switch someone can flip.
